title: Arcadia
events_chronological: In the schoolroom at Sidley Park, thirteen-year-old Thomasina Coverly asks her tutor Septimus Hodge what a carnal embrace is, having overheard about him and Mrs Chater in the gazebo.
The poet Ezra Chater challenges Septimus to a duel over his wife, and Septimus talks him out of it by promising a favourable review.
Lady Croom quarrels with the landscape gardener Richard Noakes over his plan to replace the park with a picturesque wilderness and a hermitage.
Septimus writes a savage review of Chater's poem while a house guest, Lord Byron, borrows books from the library and leaves the country.
Chater and Captain Brice sail for the West Indies with Mrs Chater, and Chater dies there of a monkey bite.
Thomasina works out an iterated method for drawing natural shapes and grasps that heat only ever goes one way.
On the eve of her seventeenth birthday Thomasina asks Septimus to teach her to waltz, and kisses him.
Thomasina dies that night when her bedroom burns.
Septimus becomes the hermit of Sidley Park and fills the hermitage with equations until he dies.
In the present day, Hannah Jarvis works in the same room on a book about the hermit and the collapse of the Romantic imagination.
Bernard Nightingale arrives hunting a scandal and decides that Byron killed Chater in a duel and fled the country for it.
Valentine Coverly, a biologist, is fitting an iterated algorithm to two centuries of grouse-shooting records kept in the house.
Bernard announces his Byron theory in a lecture and is taken up by the newspapers.
Valentine recognises that the mathematics in Thomasina's lesson book is a version of what he is doing himself.
Hannah proves that Chater died abroad of a monkey bite, and Bernard's theory collapses in public.
Hannah identifies the hermit as Septimus from a figure drawn into the gardener's book of plans.
In the last scene the two centuries occupy the room together, and both couples waltz among each other's papers.
syuzhet_notes: The scenes alternate between the early nineteenth century and the present, both moving forward in their own time, until the last scene, in which the two periods are on stage simultaneously. Each modern scene works on the evidence the preceding historical scene has just produced, so the pairing is explanation rather than contrast.
fabula_notes: The chronology of the earlier strand is fixed by the dates in the play's own documents. The hermit's identity and the girl's death are established only in the modern strand, but the events themselves belong where they are placed here.
